experiences.title: Senior Engineering Consultant

Drove technical change management across engineering, QA, and delivery leadership, translating infrastructure risks into concrete decisions, milestones, validation plans, and release criteria.
Built a system inventory and dependency map spanning serverless services, shared libraries, source repositories, architectures, and invocation paths to expose hidden blast radius before migration.
Diagnosed production failures across distributed, event-driven workflows by tracing data through APIs, serverless functions, application logs, databases, and upstream and downstream systems.

Converted an ambiguous runtime-upgrade mandate into an executable modernization program with structured backlog items, risk tiers, implementation options, executive briefs, and operational requirements.

Presented architecture, delivery, and risk tradeoffs to technical and non-technical stakeholders while coordinating decisions across teams with competing priorities.

projects.name: FynX
description: FynX is a reactive incremental-computation library for Python, designed for application state and any other problem where results must remain synchronized with inputs that change over time. You describe a graph of changing values and the computations derived from them; when an input changes, FynX recomputes the affected part of the graph, keeps unobserved work lazy, and notifies subscribers where a result meets the outside world.

Inspired by MobX and functional reactive programming, FynX works with ordinary Python functions and has zero core dependencies. It can be introduced around a single computation without requiring the rest of the project to adopt a new architecture.

projects.name: TRELLIS-BOX
projects.tagline: Microsoft's TRELLIS image-to-3D pipeline, containerized for consumer GPUs
description: This repository packages Microsoft's TRELLIS image-to-3D pipeline into containers you can actually run on consumer hardware without spending an afternoon fighting dependencies. The goal is simple: run it locally, ungated, on a single consumer GPU — with the defaults chosen so nothing forces you through a license wall or a datacenter card just to get a 3D model out.

Both builds are tuned for high-quality generation on a 12 GB GPU. Microsoft's TRELLIS.2 repository specifies a 24 GB minimum, tested on A100/H100 hardware; the memory work here targets a 12 GB local runtime through FP16 on v1, plus lazy model scheduling and flow-block offload on v2. Docker, an NVIDIA GPU, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit are the only requirements.

highlights.label: TRELLIS/
highlights.detail: The original Streamlit app, tuned for lower VRAM with FP16 mixed precision (~50% memory savings) and automatic GLB export. Runs at localhost:8501.

highlights.label: TRELLIS.2/
highlights.detail: The newer O-Voxel/PBR pipeline with a Gradio interface and a dedicated texturing app. Runs at localhost:7860.

projects.name: Homeworld
projects.tagline: A transactional runtime for your personal computing environment
description: Homeworld makes setting up a machine feel like restoring it rather than rebuilding it. Your shell configuration, the scripts living in ~/bin on exactly one computer, the packages you always install, the tools you clone from GitHub — Homeworld gathers them into one Git repository and makes every machine you own match it. Change something on your desktop, push, run `homeworld update --install` on your laptop, and get back to work.

Because every change builds off to the side and activates as a transaction, a broken install can't take your working environment with it. If a build fails, nothing changed. If it succeeds and you regret it, one command puts the previous environment back.

highlights.label: update --install
highlights.detail: Applies your machine's full configuration and installs everything it depends on in one command.

highlights.label: rollback
highlights.detail: Every change builds off to the side and only activates as a transaction — a broken build never touches your working environment, and one command reverts a bad install.

projects.name: Dogescript
projects.tagline: JavaScript for the moon — a Doge-themed language that compiles to real JS
description: Dogescript is an esoteric language that compiles to real JavaScript, swapping conventional syntax for Doge-meme vocabulary — such, much, very, rly, wow — while keeping actual functions, conditionals, and scoping underneath. It's playful on the surface, but it's a real compiler: valid Dogescript produces valid, runnable JavaScript.

I'm a maintainer of the project, where I've contributed to language design and architecture, modernized its build and tooling stack, and built out its testing suite and testing conventions from the ground up.

projects.name: Personal Website
projects.tagline: Software engineering portfolio and component system
description: Web engineers sometimes joke that beautiful websites are large and ugly websites are small. Once you start caring about accessibility, responsive imagery, design systems, performance budgets, and polished interactions, bytes have a way of accumulating. This repository is my answer to that bit of engineering folklore.

It contains my personal website and the component system that powers it. While intentionally small enough to inspect in an afternoon, it's built with the same standards I bring to a production product surface: semantic design tokens, isolated components, accessible interactions, responsive image handling, critical CSS, Storybook documentation, and reproducible performance checks.

The end result is a static production build with a near-perfect Lighthouse score (github's servers permitting), deployed to GitHub Pages and accompanied by a pre-built Storybook, making the entire component library inspectable without cloning the repository. This site behaves like an elaborate application, yet loads like a small static document.
